Vilely
VYLE-lee
adv. (basely; in a manner showing contempt, shamefully)
From vile, Old French vil, from Latin vilis, cheap, of little worth, with the adverbial -ly. The Hebrew gaal means to defile or treat as foul.

Biblical Definition

David's lament over Saul and Jonathan curses the mountain where they fell: “Ye mountains of Gilboa, let there be no dew, neither let there be rain, upon you, nor fields of offerings: for there the shield of the mighty is vilely cast away, the shield of Saul, as though he had not been anointed with oil” (2 Samuel 1:21). To be vilely cast away is to be thrown aside as worthless. The shield of a king, the emblem of Israel's defence, lay abandoned on a hillside like refuse, and David's grief fastens on the dishonour of it: as though he had not been anointed with oil. What is remarkable is who is speaking. Saul had hunted David for years, and David had twice spared him. Now the man with every reason for satisfaction composes a public lament, forbids rejoicing in Gath and Askelon, and calls Saul the beauty of Israel: “The beauty of Israel is slain upon thy high places: how are the mighty fallen!” (2 Samuel 1:19). The song ends where it began: “How are the mighty fallen, and the weapons of war perished!” (2 Samuel 1:27). Grief for the fall of the LORD's anointed, even an enemy, is a mark of a godly man.

Webster (1828): VILELY, basely; meanly; shamefully; VILE, base; mean; worthless; despicable.

Key Scripture

2Sa 1:21 — "Ye mountains of Gilboa, let there be no dew, neither let there be rain, upon you, nor fields of offerings: for there the shield of the mighty is vilely cast away, the shield of Saul, as though he had not been anointed with oil."

2Sa 1:19 — "The beauty of Israel is slain upon thy high places: how are the mighty fallen!"

2Sa 1:27 — "How are the mighty fallen, and the weapons of war perished!"

Modern Corruption

The fall of an enemy is received with satisfaction and published as vindication, where David composed a lament and forbade his people to rejoice.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is David's conduct over the body of the man who had hunted him: he mourned, he honoured the office, he suppressed the news in Philistine streets, and he had the lament taught to the children of Judah.

The temptation is strongest where the enmity was real. A rival discredited, an opponent exposed, a persecutor fallen: the flesh calls this vindication and wants it broadcast. Scripture forbids it. Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth, says Proverbs, lest the LORD see it and turn away His wrath from him. David's song over Gilboa is the practical shape of loving an enemy, written by a man who had every human warrant for the opposite.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

From Latin vilis, cheap; Hebrew gaal, to defile; 2 Samuel 1:21 mourns Saul's shield vilely cast away.

expand to see more

Latin vilis, cheap or of little worth, gives vile and vilely.

Hebrew gaal, to defile or treat as foul.

2 Samuel 1:21 is the only occurrence of vilely in the Authorized Version.

The dishonour is sharpened by the words as though he had not been anointed.

The lament was composed by the man Saul had hunted for years.
